claim: MLL fusion proteins associate with the HBO1 histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex through their trithorax homology domain 2 (THD2) in various human cell lines.
source: Here, we showed that leukemic MLL fusion proteins associate with the HBO1 histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complex through their trithorax homology domain 2 (THD2) in various human cell lines.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript including mass spectrometry and immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: MLL proteins associated with the HBO1 complex through multiple contacts mediated mainly by the ING4/5 and PHF16 subunits in a chromatin-bound context where histone H3 lysine 4 tri-methylation marks were present.
source: MLL proteins associated with the HBO1 complex through multiple contacts mediated mainly by the ING4/5 and PHF16 subunits in a chromatin-bound context where histone H3 lysine 4 tri-methylation marks were present.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation and ChIP experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: MLL-ELL particularly depended on the THD2-mediated association with the HBO1 complex for leukemic transformation among many MLL fusions.
source: Of the many MLL fusions, MLL-ELL particularly depended on the THD2-mediated association with the HBO1 complex for leukemic transformation.
evidence: This is supported by transformation assays shown in Figure 1 demonstrating that MLL-ELL requires THD2 for transformation.

claim: The C-terminal portion of ELL provided a binding platform for multiple factors including AF4, EAF1, and p53.
source: The C-terminal portion of ELL provided a binding platform for multiple factors including AF4, EAF1, and p53.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figures 4-6 demonstrating interactions between ELL and these factors.

claim: MLL-ELL activated gene expression in murine hematopoietic progenitors by loading an AF4/ENL/P-TEFb (AEP) complex onto the target promoters wherein the HBO1 complex promoted the association with AEP complex over EAF1 and p53.
source: MLL-ELL activated gene expression in murine hematopoietic progenitors by loading an AF4/ENL/P-TEFb (AEP) complex onto the target promoters wherein the HBO1 complex promoted the association with AEP complex over EAF1 and p53.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR and transformation assays shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: The NUP98-HBO1 fusion protein exerted its oncogenic properties via interaction with MLL but not its intrinsic HAT activity.
source: Moreover, the NUP98-HBO1 fusion protein exerted its oncogenic properties via interaction with MLL but not its intrinsic HAT activity.
evidence: This is supported by transformation assays with HAT-dead mutants shown in Figure 7.

claim: The interaction between the HBO1 complex and MLL is an important nexus in leukemic transformation, which may serve as a therapeutic target for drug development.
source: Thus, the interaction between the HBO1 complex and MLL is an important nexus in leukemic transformation, which may serve as a therapeutic target for drug development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents speculation about therapeutic applications.

claim: MLL is a transcriptional maintenance factor that upregulates homeobox (HOX) genes in development.
source: MLL (also known as KMT2A) is a transcriptional maintenance factor that upregulates homeobox (HOX) genes in development (Yu et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 1998.

claim: Chromosomal translocations generate fusion genes encoding various MLL fusion proteins with more than 80 different partners to induce leukemia.
source: Chromosomal translocations generate fusion genes encoding various MLL fusion proteins with more than 80 different partners to induce leukemia (Meyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meyer et al., 2018.

claim: MLL fusion proteins cause uncontrolled self-renewal by constitutively activating various oncogenic genes (e.g., HOXA9, MEIS1), whose expression is normally restricted in immature precursors such as hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
source: MLL fusion proteins cause uncontrolled self-renewal by constitutively activating various oncogenic genes (e.g., HOXA9, MEIS1), whose expression is normally restricted in immature precursors such as hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Krivtsov et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krivtsov et al., 2006.

claim: MLL fusion proteins form a complex with MENIN.
source: MLL fusion proteins form a complex with MENIN (Yokoyama et al., 2005; Yokoyama et al., 2004), which leads to further association with LEGDF (Yokoyama and Cleary, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yokoyama et al., 2005 and Yokoyama et al., 2004.

claim: MLL fusion proteins bind to their target chromatin through the CXXC domain of MLL, which specifically recognizes unmethylated CpGs.
source: MLL fusion proteins bind to their target chromatin through the CXXC domain of MLL, which specifically recognizes unmethylated CpGs, and the PWWP domain of LEDGF, which selectively binds to di/tri-methylated histone H3 lysine 36 (H3K36me2/3) (Ayton et al., 2004; Birke et al., 2002; Pradeepa et al., 2012; van Nuland et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ayton et al., 2004; Birke et al., 2002; Pradeepa et al., 2012; van Nuland et al., 2013.

claim: The PWWP domain of LEDGF selectively binds to di/tri-methylated histone H3 lysine 36 (H3K36me2/3).
source: MLL fusion proteins bind to their target chromatin through the CXXC domain of MLL, which specifically recognizes unmethylated CpGs, and the PWWP domain of LEDGF, which selectively binds to di/tri-methylated histone H3 lysine 36 (H3K36me2/3) (Ayton et al., 2004; Birke et al., 2002; Pradeepa et al., 2012; van Nuland et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ayton et al., 2004; Birke et al., 2002; Pradeepa et al., 2012; van Nuland et al., 2013.

claim: The CXXC and PWWP domains constitute the minimum targeting module (MTM) which can stably bind to the human MLL target gene promoters (e.g., HOXA9).
source: The CXXC and PWWP domains constitute the minimum targeting module (MTM) which can stably bind to the human MLL target gene promoters (e.g., HOXA9) (Okuda et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Okuda et al., 2014.

claim: Most MLL fusion-mediated leukemia cases are caused by the fusions with the AF4 family (e.g., AF4 also known as AFF1, AF5Q31 also known as AFF4) and ENL family (e.g., ENL also known as MLLT1, AF9 also known as MLLT3).
source: Although MLL fuses with a variety of partners, most MLL fusion-mediated leukemia cases are caused by the fusions with the AF4 family (e.g., AF4 also known as AFF1, AF5Q31 also known as AFF4) and ENL family (e.g., ENL also known as MLLT1, AF9 also known as MLLT3) (Meyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meyer et al., 2018.

claim: AF4 family proteins form a biochemically stable complex with ENL family proteins and the P-TEFb elongation factor (composed of CDK9 and CyclinT1/2), termed AEP complex.
source: AF4 family proteins form a biochemically stable complex with ENL family proteins and the P-TEFb elongation factor (composed of CDK9 and CyclinT1/2), which we termed AEP complex (as in AF4 family/ENL family/P-TEFb complex) (Yokoyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yokoyama et al., 2010.

claim: AF4 family proteins recruit the SL1 complex.
source: AF4 family proteins recruit the SL1 complex (Okuda et al., 2015), which is composed of TBP and the TAF1A/B/C/D subunits and is known to initiate ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I (Goodfellow and Zomerdijk, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Okuda et al., 2015 and Goodfellow and Zomerdijk, 2013.

claim: The SL1 complex is composed of TBP and the TAF1A/B/C/D subunits and is known to initiate ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I.
source: AF4 family proteins recruit the SL1 complex (Okuda et al., 2015), which is composed of TBP and the TAF1A/B/C/D subunits and is known to initiate ribosomal RNA transcription by RNA polymerase I (Goodfellow and Zomerdijk, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goodfellow and Zomerdijk, 2013.

claim: An artificial construct of MTM fused to the binding platform for SL1 activated the murine Hoxa9 gene and transformed hematopoietic progenitors (HPCs).
source: An artificial construct of MTM fused to the binding platform for SL1 activated the murine Hoxa9 gene and transformed hematopoietic progenitors (HPCs) (Okuda et al., 2015), indicating that the AF4 family protein activates RNA polymerase II (RNAP2)-dependent transcription, presumably by loading TBP onto the target promoters via SL1.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Okuda et al., 2015.

claim: HBO1 is a member of the MYST HAT family responsible for histone H3 lysine 14 acetylation (H3K14ac) when complexed with BRPF family proteins.
source: HBO1 is a member of the MYST HAT family responsible for histone H3 lysine 14 acetylation (H3K14ac) when complexed with BRPF family proteins, while it mainly acetylates histone H4 lysine 5/8/12 when complexed with JADE family proteins (Lalonde et al., 2013; Mishima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lalonde et al., 2013 and Mishima et al., 2011.

claim: HBO1 mainly acetylates histone H4 lysine 5/8/12 when complexed with JADE family proteins.
source: HBO1 is a member of the MYST HAT family responsible for histone H3 lysine 14 acetylation (H3K14ac) when complexed with BRPF family proteins, while it mainly acetylates histone H4 lysine 5/8/12 when complexed with JADE family proteins (Lalonde et al., 2013; Mishima et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lalonde et al., 2013 and Mishima et al., 2011.

claim: HBO1 was recently identified as a therapeutic vulnerability of leukemia stem cells by genetic screening.
source: HBO1 was recently identified as a therapeutic vulnerability of leukemia stem cells by genetic screening (Au et al., 2020; MacPherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Au et al., 2020 and MacPherson et al., 2020.

claim: MLL fusion proteins confer unlimited self-renewal ability, leading to the immortalization of HPCs.
source: MLL fusion proteins confer unlimited self-renewal ability, leading to the immortalization of HPCs (Lavau et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lavau et al., 1997.

claim: MLL-ELL is among the frequently observed MLL fusions associated with acute myelogenous leukemia.
source: MLL-ELL is among the frequently observed MLL fusions associated with acute myelogenous leukemia (Meyer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Meyer et al., 2018.

claim: MLL-ELL transformed HPCs, as previously reported, featured vigorous colony-forming capacities at the third and fourth passages, and showed elevated Hoxa9 expression at the first and second passages.
source: MLL-ELL transformed HPCs, as previously reported (DiMartino et al., 2000; Luo et al., 2001), featured vigorous colony-forming capacities at the third and fourth passages, and showed elevated Hoxa9 expression at the first and second passages.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1A and citations to DiMartino et al., 2000 and Luo et al., 2001.

claim: A deletion mutant of MLL-ELL lacking THD2 failed to transform.
source: A deletion mutant lacking THD2 failed to transform (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), underscoring the biological significance of THD2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A minimalistic artificial construct of HA-tagged MTM fused to an intact Occludin homology domain (OHD) of ELL failed to transform HPCs.
source: A minimalistic artificial construct of HA-tagged MTM fused to an intact Occludin homology domain (OHD) of ELL failed to transform HPCs (Figure 1A, see MTMh-ELL″), whereas inclusion of THD2 to MTM (hereafter denoted as MTMT) caused constitutive activation of Hoxa9 and immortalization of HPCs (Figure 1A, see MTMTh-ELL″).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Inclusion of THD2 to MTM (denoted as MTMT) caused constitutive activation of Hoxa9 and immortalization of HPCs.
source: A minimalistic artificial construct of HA-tagged MTM fused to an intact Occludin homology domain (OHD) of ELL failed to transform HPCs (Figure 1A, see MTMh-ELL″), whereas inclusion of THD2 to MTM (hereafter denoted as MTMT) caused constitutive activation of Hoxa9 and immortalization of HPCs (Figure 1A, see MTMTh-ELL″).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MLL-ELL transforms HPCs through THD2-mediated functions.
source: These results indicate that MLL-ELL transforms HPCs through THD2-mediated functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An MLL-AF6 fusion construct, in which MLL is fused to the RA1 and RA2 domains of AF6, fully transformed HPCs as previously reported.
source: An MLL-AF6 fusion construct, in which MLL is fused to the RA1 and RA2 domains of AF6 (see MLL-AF6′), fully transformed HPCs as previously reported (Liedtke et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and a citation to Liedtke et al., 2010.

claim: The minimalistic MTM-AF6 fusion construct activated Hoxa9 expression in the early passages but produced modest numbers of colonies in later passages.
source: The minimalistic MTM-AF6 fusion construct (Figure 1B, see MTMh-AF6′) activated Hoxa9 expression in the early passages but produced modest numbers of colonies in later passages, while the inclusion of THD2 (Figure 1B, see MTMTh-AF6′) conferred much more vigorous transforming capacities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Inclusion of THD2 in MTM-AF6 conferred much more vigorous transforming capacities.
source: The minimalistic MTM-AF6 fusion construct (Figure 1B, see MTMh-AF6′) activated Hoxa9 expression in the early passages but produced modest numbers of colonies in later passages, while the inclusion of THD2 (Figure 1B, see MTMTh-AF6′) conferred much more vigorous transforming capacities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of THD2 from a PWWP-MLL-AF6 fusion construct containing the residues 641/1267 of MLL abrogated its transforming ability.
source: Deletion of THD2 from a PWWP-MLL-AF6 fusion construct containing the residues 641/1267 of MLL (P′641/1267h-AF6′) abrogated its transforming ability, suggesting that MLL-AF6 requires THD2 to exert its full transforming potential (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MLL-AF6 requires THD2 to exert its full transforming potential.
source: Deletion of THD2 from a PWWP-MLL-AF6 fusion construct containing the residues 641/1267 of MLL (P′641/1267h-AF6′) abrogated its transforming ability, suggesting that MLL-AF6 requires THD2 to exert its full transforming potential (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An MLL-AF6′ construct lacking THD2 immortalized HPCs albeit less efficiently compared to MLL-AF6′.
source: Nonetheless, an MLL-AF6′ construct lacking THD2 immortalized HPCs albeit less efficiently compared to MLL-AF6′ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, see MLL-AF6′ ΔTHD2), suggestive of some compensatory functions mediated by other MLL structures retained in MLL-AF6′ but missing in P′641/1267h-AF6′ (i.e., the residues 1/640 and 1268/1395).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MLL-AF10 showed a similar trend to MLL-AF6 in terms of THD2 dependency.
source: MLL-AF10 showed a similar trend, in line with our previous report (Okuda et al., 2017; Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B, and a citation to Okuda et al., 2017.

claim: The oncogenic properties of MLL-ENL were not severely affected by the loss of THD2 in terms of colony-forming capacity.
source: In contrast, the oncogenic properties of MLL-ENL were not severely affected by the loss of THD2 in terms of colony-forming capacity (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Okuda et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and a citation to Okuda et al., 2014.

claim: The colony morphology of immortalized cells transformed by the MTMh-ENL construct was more differentiated compared to that of MTMTh-ENL′-ICs.
source: However, the colony morphology of immortalized cells (ICs) transformed by the MTMh-ENL construct (MTMh-ENL′-ICs) was more differentiated compared to that of MTMTh-ENL′-ICs (Figure 1C), suggesting that THD2 is required to block differentiation to some extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: THD2 is required to block differentiation to some extent in MLL-ENL transformed cells.
source: However, the colony morphology of immortalized cells (ICs) transformed by the MTMh-ENL construct (MTMh-ENL′-ICs) was more differentiated compared to that of MTMTh-ENL′-ICs (Figure 1C), suggesting that THD2 is required to block differentiation to some extent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Leukemogenesis in vivo was compromised by the deletion of THD2 for MLL-AF6, -AF10, and -ENL.
source: Leukemogenesis in vivo was compromised by the deletion of THD2 for MLL-AF6, -AF10, and -ENL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MLL fusion proteins rely on THD2-mediated functions for leukemic transformation to varying degrees depending on their fusion partners.
source: These results indicate that MLL fusion proteins rely on THD2-mediated functions for leukemic transformation to varying degrees depending on their fusion partners.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Among the MLL fusions tested, MLL-ELL most heavily relies on THD2-mediated functions.
source: Among the MLL fusions tested, MLL-ELL most heavily relies on THD2-mediated functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Components of the HBO1 complex including HBO1, PHF16, MEAF6, and ING5 were detected in the purified materials from THD2-containing proteins.
source: Components of the HBO1 complex including HBO1, PHF16 (also known as JADE3), MEAF6, and ING5 were detected in the purified materials (Avvakumov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A and a citation to Avvakumov et al., 2012.

claim: fGAL4-MLL 869/1124 co-precipitated with HBO1 complex components but not with exogenously expressed AF4.
source: Immunoprecipitation-western blotting (IP-WB) analysis confirmed that fGAL4-MLL 869/1124 co-precipitated with HBO1 complex components but not with exogenously expressed AF4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A series of MTMT fusion proteins were associated with HBO1 and PHF16, while the respective MTM fusion proteins were not.
source: A series of MTMT fusion proteins were associated with HBO1 and PHF16, while the respective MTM fusion proteins were not (Figure 2C), confirming that THD2 mediates interaction with the HBO1 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: THD2 mediates interaction with the HBO1 complex.
source: A series of MTMT fusion proteins were associated with HBO1 and PHF16, while the respective MTM fusion proteins were not (Figure 2C), confirming that THD2 mediates interaction with the HBO1 complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The residues 869/1124 of MLL contain the major binding domains for the HBO1 complex.
source: Domain mapping analysis of MLL showed that the residues 869/1124 contain the major binding domains for the HBO1 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: fGAL4-MLL 1052/1124 co-precipitated with the HBO1 complex components after DNaseI treatment, indicating that association of MLL and HBO1 is not mediated by DNA.
source: Moreover, fGAL4-MLL 1052/1124 co-precipitated with the HBO1 complex components after DNaseI treatment, indicating that association of MLL and HBO1 is not mediated by DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A small amount of HBO1 co-precipitated with the MLL proteins lacking the THD2 domain, suggesting that there is a secondary binding domain for the HBO1 complex outside of THD2.
source: It should be noted that a small amount of HBO1 co-precipitated with the MLL proteins lacking the THD2 domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, see fMLL ΔFP ΔTHD2 and fMLL-ENL ΔTHD2), suggesting that there is a secondary binding domain for the HBO1 complex outside of THD2, which may account for the moderate effects of THD2 deletion from the full-length MLL fusion constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Interaction between endogenous MLL proteins and HBO1 was confirmed in leukemia cell lines such as HB1119 and REH.
source: Interaction between endogenous MLL proteins and HBO1 was confirmed in leukemia cell lines such as HB1119 and REH (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: HBO1 complex components colocalized with MLL-ENL at the MLL target genes (e.g., MYC, HOXA9, and MYB) in a genome-wide manner.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) followed by deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) of HB1119 cells, which endogenously express MLL-ENL, demonstrated that HBO1 complex components colocalized with MLL-ENL at the MLL target genes (e.g., MYC, HOXA9, and MYB) in a genome-wide manner (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Kat7/KAT7 (the gene encoding HBO1) is required for the proliferation of various MLL fusion-ICs.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated sgRNA competition assays demonstrated that Kat7/KAT7 (the gene encoding HBO1) is required for the proliferation of various MLL fusion-ICs (Figure 2F) and in human leukemia cell lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The HBO1 complex associates with multiple MLL fusion proteins and plays a critical role in the maintenance of leukemia stem cells.
source: These results are consistent with the recent reports, which showed that the HBO1 complex associates with multiple MLL fusion proteins and plays a critical role in the maintenance of leukemia stem cells (Au et al., 2020; MacPherson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Au et al., 2020 and MacPherson et al., 2020.

claim: MLL fusion proteins associate with the HBO1 complex through THD2 at the target promoters.
source: Taken together, MLL fusion proteins associate with the HBO1 complex through THD2 at the target promoters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MLL localizes at the transcription start sites (TSSs) of CpG-rich genes including RPL13A, MYC, and CDKN2C.
source: MLL localizes at the transcription start sites (TSSs) of CpG-rich genes including RPL13A, MYC, and CDKN2C (Okuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A and a citation to Okuda et al., 2017.

claim: Distribution of the HBO1 complex was enriched at promoter proximal transcribed regions (0–2 kb from the TSS).
source: Distribution of the HBO1 complex was enriched at promoter proximal transcribed regions (0–2 kb from the TSS) (Figure 3B) consistent with a previous report (Avvakumov et al., 2012), suggesting its implication in transcription initiation/elongation.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Avvakumov et al., 2012.

claim: The HBO1 complex was localized at the MLL-occupied promoters in a genome-wide manner similarly to that in HB1119 cells.
source: The HBO1 complex was localized at the MLL-occupied promoters in a genome-wide manner similarly to that in HB1119 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: MLL associates with the MOZ complex and yet-to-be activated RNAP2 whose heptapeptide repeats are not phosphorylated (RNAP2 non-P) on target promoters.
source: We previously showed that MLL associates with the MOZ complex and yet-to-be activated RNAP2 whose heptapeptide repeats are not phosphorylated (RNAP2 non-P) on target promoters, and that it colocalizes with various ENL-containing complexes including the AEP and DOT1L complexes (Miyamoto et al., 2020; Okuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miyamoto et al., 2020 and Okuda et al., 2017.

claim: MLL colocalizes with various ENL-containing complexes including the AEP and DOT1L complexes.
source: We previously showed that MLL associates with the MOZ complex and yet-to-be activated RNAP2 whose heptapeptide repeats are not phosphorylated (RNAP2 non-P) on target promoters, and that it colocalizes with various ENL-containing complexes including the AEP and DOT1L complexes (Miyamoto et al., 2020; Okuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miyamoto et al., 2020 and Okuda et al., 2017.

claim: The ChIP signal intensities of MLL were highly correlated with those of HBO1, MOZ, and RNAP2 non-P.
source: The ChIP signal intensities of MLL were highly correlated with those of HBO1, MOZ, and RNAP2 non-P (Figure 3C), supporting the functional interactions of MLL with those MLL-associated factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ChIP signals of AEP (e.g., AF4, ENL) and SL1 (e.g., TAF1C) are weakly correlated with that of MLL, presumably because AEP and SL1 are indirectly recruited to MLL target promoters in a context-dependent manner.
source: The ChIP signals of AEP (e.g., AF4, ENL) and SL1 (e.g., TAF1C) are weakly correlated with that of MLL, presumably because AEP and SL1 are indirectly recruited to MLL target promoters in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Depletion of MLL by the knockout of KMT2A reduced the expression of MYC and CDKN2C.
source: Depletion of MLL by the knockout of KMT2A (the gene encoding MLL) reduced the expression of MYC and CDKN2C (Figure 3D,E), as previously reported (Miyamoto et al., 2020), and caused a marked reduction in the ChIP signals of the HBO1 complex components (i.e., PHF16, MEAF6) at the MYC and CDKN2C loci (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E and a citation to Miyamoto et al., 2020.

claim: Depletion of MLL caused a marked reduction in the ChIP signals of the HBO1 complex components (i.e., PHF16, MEAF6) at the MYC and CDKN2C loci.
source: Depletion of MLL by the knockout of KMT2A (the gene encoding MLL) reduced the expression of MYC and CDKN2C (Figure 3D,E), as previously reported (Miyamoto et al., 2020), and caused a marked reduction in the ChIP signals of the HBO1 complex components (i.e., PHF16, MEAF6) at the MYC and CDKN2C loci (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The HBO1 complex is presumed to target the chromatin containing histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me3) marks to which the PHD finger of the ING5 subunit specifically binds.
source: The HBO1 complex is presumed to target the chromatin containing histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4me3) marks to which the PHD finger of the ING5 subunit specifically binds (Champagne et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Champagne et al., 2008.

claim: H3K4me3 marks were substantially reduced at the MYC and CDKN2C promoters as they were presumably provided by MLL in part.
source: H3K4me3 marks were substantially reduced at the MYC and CDKN2C promoters as they were presumably provided by MLL in part.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The decreased presence of the HBO1 complex may be due to the reduced H3K4me3 marks.
source: These results suggest that the decreased presence of the HBO1 complex may be due to the reduced H3K4me3 marks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Transient expression of a THD2-containing MLL construct (MTMTh) did not rescue the recruitment of the HBO1 complex onto the MYC promoter, suggesting that H3K4 methylation is a prerequisite for the recruitment of the HBO1 complex.
source: Transient expression of a THD2-containing MLL construct (MTMTh) did not rescue the recruitment of the HBO1 complex onto the MYC promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that H3K4 methylation is a prerequisite for the recruitment of the HBO1 complex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ChIP signals of AEP/SL1 components (i.e., ENL, CCNT1, AF4, and TAF1C) were reduced at the MYC and CDKN2C loci in MLL-deficient cells.
source: In addition, the ChIP signals of AEP/SL1 components (i.e., ENL, CCNT1, AF4, and TAF1C) were also reduced at these loci (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MLL recruits the HBO1, AEP, and SL1 complexes to the MYC and CDKN2C promoters in part via H3K4 methylation.
source: These results indicate that MLL recruits the HBO1, AEP, and SL1 complexes to the MYC and CDKN2C promoters in part via H3K4 methylation.
